assumption: One experienced generalist, 10 working days over two calendar weeks, roughly 60 focused production hours plus 10 hours for testing and outreach. Scope estimates below are Steam Discovery proposals, not measured development times. AI-assisted means code, iteration and production help; runtime generative AI is not required.
releaseConstraint: A playable build in 14 days is not a promise of a Steam launch. For a first release, Valve documents a 30-day waiting period after the application fee and at least two weeks of a public Coming Soon page. Store/build review and demo setup need their own schedule. Verify your account and application state before choosing a launch date.

concepts.title: Desk Lighthouse
concepts.pitch: A tiny lighthouse sits at the edge of your screen. Each completed focus session guides a different paper boat home.
concepts.spin: Progress is an evolving harbor with finite hand-authored arrivals, rather than a second idle economy to manage.
scope: One resizable window and optional always-on-top mode
One timer, one save slot, six boats and three harbor upgrades
One 25-minute ritual plus a fast preview mode
cuts: No calendar accounts, desktop injection or cloud sync
No procedural dialogue, pets economy or multiplayer
concepts.aiHelp: Scaffold timer state, save migrations and UI variants; generate deterministic test cases for pause, sleep and resume.
concepts.humanBottleneck: Comfort, idle CPU use, sound restraint and whether interruption feels pleasant.
concepts.clip: An empty harbor becomes a lit miniature town while the real work stays visible.
concepts.channel: Cozy and productivity curators; a short desk setup clip linked to an honest playable sample.
concepts.test: Five remote workers use it during one real focus session. Record voluntary second-session use and interruptions they disliked.
concepts.stop: Stop if the app repeatedly steals attention or its appeal disappears when the novelty clip ends.
risks: OS-specific window behavior consumes the sprint
Existing desktop bundles are strong competition
concepts.commercial: Treat the two-week output as a comfort test. A shippable desktop utility requires more compatibility coverage.

concepts.title: Lost Luggage League
concepts.pitch: Pack the wrong suitcases for the right passengers: every item changes the next automated baggage-carousel duel.
concepts.spin: The opponent is visible before packing. Rearranging a small suitcase is the decision, not collecting hundreds of items.
scope: One 4×4 grid, eight items, three enemies
Five encounters with deterministic combat
One visible synergy and one counter per item family
cuts: No rarity economy, procedural map or meta-progression
concepts.aiHelp: Implement grid placement tests, combat logs and a seeded balance simulator; propose item combinations for human review.
concepts.humanBottleneck: A readable and interesting choice must survive the very small content pool.
concepts.clip: Rotate a ridiculous umbrella and turn a losing suitcase into a winning combination.
concepts.channel: Inventory and autobattler creators who explain decisions in long-form videos.
concepts.test: Ask ten players to explain why they changed their layout before the third encounter; log distinct successful arrangements.
concepts.stop: Stop if one obvious layout solves every encounter or players cannot explain a synergy.
risks: A strategy audience expects depth beyond a funny skin
concepts.commercial: Two weeks can test one ruleset, not compete with an established item ecosystem.

concepts.title: Bureau of Gravity
concepts.pitch: Shred obsolete gravity permits until the office furniture starts floating; buy upgrades that make the mess wonderfully worse.
concepts.spin: Progress visibly transforms one room and ends with a controlled comic disaster.
scope: One repeatable input and three upgrade branches
One room with staged transformations
15–25 minutes of progression and a real ending
cuts: No prestige loop, live economy or infinite content
No general physics simulation; use authored stages
concepts.aiHelp: Generate UI scaffolding and offline progression simulations; draft tuning tables and edge-case tests.
concepts.humanBottleneck: Pacing, sound, feedback and avoiding a dead stretch between upgrades.
concepts.clip: A dull desk becomes an orbiting stationery storm in a single before-and-after shot.
concepts.channel: Incremental-game communities where self-promotion is allowed and small creators who finish short games.
concepts.test: Observe ten complete sessions. Locate the first boredom or confusion point; measure how many finish voluntarily.
concepts.stop: Cut progression if an upgrade does not change what the player can see or decide.
risks: Fast content consumption and refund exposure
A loop can be satisfying in a clip but tedious to play
concepts.commercial: Potentially a complete tiny game only with an already-ready Steam application, licensed assets and a stable build. Price after testing the finished experience.

concepts.title: Midnight Returns Desk
concepts.pitch: Process returns from customers who insist impossible products are working as intended.
concepts.spin: Accepting an item changes the rules for later customers, so a familiar inspection job becomes comic cause and effect.
scope: One counter, six products and eight customers
Inspect, stamp and place as the only verbs
One authored shift with two endings
cuts: No walkable town, staff management or stock economy
No generated conversations or voice service dependency
concepts.aiHelp: Build an authored customer-state machine, interaction prompts and localization drafts; test each rule branch.
concepts.humanBottleneck: Objects must feel tactile, and jokes need timing and legibility.
concepts.clip: A customer returns a toaster because it keeps predicting the future; the player tests it.
concepts.channel: Simulation and comedy creators; show an actual shift with a complete setup and consequence.
concepts.test: Have ten players complete a shift without explanation; record misunderstood rules and which objects they retest.
concepts.stop: Simplify if the player reads more than they touch or the premise needs a long explanation.
risks: The premise may feel like a sketch without meaningful decisions
concepts.commercial: An eight-customer slice validates interaction; it does not validate a full shop economy.

concepts.title: Night Shift: Freight 13
concepts.pitch: Sort late-night parcels in a locked freight office; one parcel learns where you are whenever you make a sound.
concepts.spin: The threat reacts to the same scanning and handling actions that earn your shift pay.
scope: One room, eight parcels and one threat state machine
One repeatable scanner interaction
A 10-minute shift and one authored climax
cuts: No city, combat, skill tree or enemy navigation outside the room
No endless anomaly catalog or online co-op
concepts.aiHelp: Scaffold interactable states, subtitles and save/reset tests; generate debug views for threat transitions.
concepts.humanBottleneck: Spatial audio, anticipation, lighting and fair readable danger.
concepts.clip: The parcel behind you repeats the sound of the scanner after you unplug it.
concepts.channel: Short-horror creators with a clean capture build and a short, spoiler-light pitch.
concepts.test: Observe whether first-time players connect noise with the threat before the climax; ask where they felt cheated.
concepts.stop: Remove random deaths and threats whose rule cannot be inferred from feedback.
risks: One-shot horror competes with abundant low-price releases
concepts.commercial: Build one satisfying shift before adding combat or a second location.

concepts.title: Museum of Alibis
concepts.pitch: Reconstruct who stole a museum exhibit by matching three contradictory visitor recordings to a tiny floor plan.
concepts.spin: Players alter the timeline and immediately see which alibis become impossible.
scope: One case, four suspects, twelve clues
A timeline and room map as the only screens
A hint ladder and one final accusation
cuts: No voice acting, freeform AI questioning or procedural mysteries
No branching narrative beyond the solved case
concepts.aiHelp: Create clue bookkeeping tools and UI code; try to falsify the timeline with generated test scenarios.
concepts.humanBottleneck: The mystery must have one fair solution. A human verifies every dependency and clue.
concepts.clip: Move an alibi by three minutes and reveal that two suspects cannot both be telling the truth.
concepts.channel: Puzzle and detective communities, then creators who enjoy explaining deductions.
concepts.test: Watch eight blind solves. Track hint usage, false ambiguity and whether the final explanation matches the evidence.
concepts.stop: Rewrite any clue that only makes sense after the author explains it.
risks: Writing and puzzle verification are the real workload
One case may not meet audience expectations for paid content
concepts.commercial: A complete short case is possible; pricing and Steam scheduling remain separate decisions.

concepts.title: Pigeon Press Pass
concepts.pitch: Photograph pigeons committing tiny civic offenses in one compact square to finish a neighborhood newspaper.
concepts.spin: The joke lives in the framing: the same bird can satisfy different assignments depending on what the photograph includes.
scope: One courtyard, three birds and six photo assignments
Simple subject and framing checks
A printable-style front page as the final reward
cuts: No open world, complex animal AI or user-uploaded images
No image recognition API; deterministic subject tagging
concepts.aiHelp: Implement framing checks, photo UI and assignment validation; automate camera-boundary tests.
concepts.humanBottleneck: Authored behavior and charming compositions; consistent assets matter more than asset quantity.
concepts.clip: A mundane bird becomes a scandalous newspaper front page through a perfectly timed photo.
concepts.channel: Cozy/photo-game creators and screenshot-led community posts with one playable square.
concepts.test: Ask players to solve assignments without arrows; record whether they take extra photos after finishing.
concepts.stop: Stop expanding if all assignments resolve from one camera angle.
risks: Charm is not a proven sales gap
Reference games have very different review scale
concepts.commercial: Validate composition and playful observation before funding additional locations.

concepts.title: One Night Courier
concepts.pitch: Route three nocturnal couriers through a small town where streets disappear when the last shop closes.
concepts.spin: The route network shrinks on a schedule visible from the start; players plan around temporary access.
scope: One graph of twelve junctions
Three couriers, four package types and six authored scenarios
A clear clock and instant replay
cuts: No traffic physics, city generator or multiplayer
No dynamic economy or dozens of buildings
concepts.aiHelp: Build the pathfinding sandbox and deterministic simulation tests; generate candidate levels for human validation.
concepts.humanBottleneck: Readable routing and scenario quality. Random maps are not automatically good puzzles.
concepts.clip: The last bridge closes as three deliveries converge, then one clever reroute saves the night.
concepts.channel: Strategy/puzzle creators who show a problem and its solution; compare two short gameplay explanations.
concepts.test: Give ten players the first three maps. Record avoidable confusion, restarts and meaningful route alternatives.
concepts.stop: Cut any system that adds visual noise without changing a route decision.
risks: Successful reference games represent years of iteration
concepts.commercial: A deterministic scenario pack is the two-week target; endless mode needs a separate validation cycle.

sprint.output: Play three comparables. Record three positive and three negative review themes with links. Build the core input and one consequence.
sprint.gate: An outsider can describe the action after a silent 10-second capture.

sprint.output: Implement start, decision, consequence, reward and reset. Use placeholder art with final collision and camera scale.
sprint.gate: Five people can finish one loop without the developer explaining controls.

sprint.output: Add the minimum authored content, audio, feedback, settings and a clear endpoint. Integrate licensed assets and review AI-assisted code.
sprint.gate: The promised moment appears in an ordinary play session, not only a staged recording.

sprint.output: Run blind tests, fix the three biggest failures, capture a truthful trailer and prepare a stable downloadable build.
sprint.gate: No progression blockers in the tested path. Declare platform and input coverage honestly.

sprint.output: Calendar buffer for feedback, outreach and platform review if already eligible. Test one clear pitch in two appropriate communities or creator niches.
sprint.gate: Choose continue, revise or stop using play behavior and attributable interest—not raw clip views.

measurement: Track visitors, demo starts, loop completion, voluntary replay and wishlists separately; these are different denominators.
Use Steam UTM links for eligible external traffic and retain each campaign window. Community posts and creator videos often overlap.
The five-, eight- and ten-player gates here are internal usability samples, not statistical proof of demand or industry benchmarks.
Before spending another month, require a written player promise, three comparables, one specific unmet complaint, and evidence that strangers want the playable experience.
aiWorkflow: Use AI for scaffolding, editor utilities, repetitive UI, test generation and first-pass localization; review the outputs.
Keep one source-controlled build. Ask AI for a bounded change with acceptance criteria, not an entire game at once.
Maintain an asset provenance and license list. Check Steam's current Content Survey for generated content shipped to players.
Treat runtime generated dialogue as a separate product feature with cost, moderation, availability and testing requirements; it is outside these slices.
AI speed does not remove tuning, taste, performance, accessibility, QA, marketing or Steam's release process.
